title: CERN Is Taking Apart the World's Biggest Atom Smasher
summary:
Have you ever taken apart a toy to make it better? Scientists in Europe are doing that right now — with the biggest machine in the world.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a giant ring, 27 kilometers around, buried underground near Geneva. It smashes tiny particles together at almost the speed of light. Scientists use it to discover what the universe is made of.

To steer those particles, the LHC uses thousands of special magnets. The most important ones are called "inner triplets" — groups of three magnets that squeeze the particle beams super tight right before they collide. The tighter the squeeze, the more collisions happen.

Now CERN, the lab that runs the LHC, has started removing 28 of these magnets. They've been working since 2005! New ones will be installed that are about 40% stronger. That means way more collisions — and way more chances to discover something new.

"It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next," says Markus Zerlauth, who leads the upgrade project.

The first new magnet should arrive in the tunnel in early 2029. So the LHC is taking a long nap — but when it wakes up, it'll be more powerful than ever.
why_it_matters: Big machines like the LHC show how teamwork and years of patience can lead to discoveries that change what we know about the universe.

background_read: CERN (a huge science laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, where scientists from many countries work together) built the LHC to study the smallest pieces of the universe.
Everything around you is made of tiny particles, and scientists learn about them by crashing them into each other and watching what flies out.
Magnets are perfect for steering particles, because charged particles curve when they move through a magnetic field — that is how the LHC keeps its beams going around the ring.
Article_Structure: WHO: CERN, the lab that runs the Large Hadron Collider, and Markus Zerlauth, who leads the upgrade project.
WHAT: Workers are taking out 28 old magnets and will install new ones that are about 40% stronger.
WHERE: Inside a 27-kilometer ring buried underground near Geneva.
WHY: Stronger magnets mean more collisions, which gives scientists more chances to discover something new.

perspectives.description: The upgrade gives scientists a much better chance of finding new particles and answering big questions about the universe.
Projects like this take many years and cost a lot of money, so some people ask whether the money could be used elsewhere.
This is how big science usually works: build a machine, learn from it, then rebuild it even better.
